overview: This file traces several connected aspects of Japanese meteorology during the Allied occupation from April 1947 to September 1949. It begins with Uruguayan requests for Tokyo temperature data, contains a major SCAP directive regulating nearly 200 Japanese weather stations, their observation duties, reporting procedures, equipment and service vessels, and then documents the international distribution of Japanese meteorological information to Mongolia, Afghanistan, Iran and Argentina. The final documents concern negotiations over transferring North Pacific ocean weather stations J and X-Ray from American to Japanese operation, including their importance for aviation and air-sea rescue, questions of reimbursement, and an estimated annual cost.

subfiles.title: Montevideo airgram requesting Tokyo temperature data
subfiles.about: Requests January 1946 and January 1947 average temperatures for Tokyo on behalf of the Uruguayan Meteorological Service.
subfiles.summary: Captain Américo Dentone sought Tokyo temperature averages as a basis for Uruguayan meteorological predictions for 1947–48. The embassy asked for a reply before May 1 if possible.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram reporting January temperature averages
subfiles.about: Supplies Tokyo's average temperatures for January 1946 and January 1947.
subfiles.summary: Replying to Department telegram 150 of April 25, Tokyo reported January averages of approximately 38.2°F in 1946 and 38.3°F in 1947. The first value appears as 18.3 in the OCR but is corrected by the subsequent Department telegram.

subfiles.title: Department telegram conveying Tokyo temperatures to Montevideo
subfiles.about: Transmits the requested Tokyo January temperature averages to the embassy in Uruguay.
subfiles.summary: The Department reported averages of 38.2°F for January 1946 and 38.3°F for January 1947. The telegram responds directly to Montevideo airgram A-146.

subfiles.title: Department request to SCAP for Tokyo weather information
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Asks SCAP to obtain the two Tokyo temperature averages requested by the embassy in Montevideo.
subfiles.summary: The Department explained that the information was for Captain Dentone and the Uruguayan Meteorological Service. It requested a telegraphic answer by May 1, 1947.

subfiles.title: Despatch transmitting revised Japanese Weather Service directive
subfiles.about: Forwards five copies of a SCAP directive rescinding and replacing earlier instructions governing Japanese weather services.
subfiles.summary: The covering despatch reports the enclosure of a new directive to the Japanese government. The cover describes it as dated September 20, while the surviving enclosed directive is SCAPIN 1782 dated September 25, 1947.

subfiles.title: SCAPIN 1782 governing the Japanese Weather Service
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.to: Japanese Government, through the Central Liaison Office, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Defines the authorized Japanese meteorological station network, observation duties, vessels, reporting requirements and approval procedures.
subfiles.summary: The directive rescinds SCAPIN 1658 and lists 197 island and district weather stations with coordinates, elevations, service codes and index numbers. It explains observation and instrument codes, authorizes limited school climatological substations and six vessels for station supply and maintenance, and requires monthly status reports to the 43d Weather Wing. Changes to stations or services require Japanese governmental, 43d Weather Wing and SCAP approval; the directive is signed by Adjutant General R. M. Levy.

subfiles.title: Incomplete Montevideo airgram A-61
subfiles.about: Records a further Montevideo request for Tokyo mean-temperature information.
subfiles.summary: Only the communications metadata survives on this page; the substantive body is absent from the OCR. The reply on the following page establishes that airgram A-61 requested mean temperatures for December and January in two successive years.

subfiles.title: Reply to Montevideo with 1947–48 Tokyo temperatures
subfiles.about: Provides Tokyo mean temperatures for December 1947 and January 1948.
subfiles.summary: The Weather Bureau supplied means of 39.4°F for December 1947 and 39.2°F for January 1948. It stated that corresponding figures for December 1946 and January 1947 were unavailable.

subfiles.title: Despatch 164 transmitting meteorological information abroad
subfiles.from: Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Requests onward transmission of four packages of Japanese meteorological data to authorities in Tehran, Ulaanbaatar, Kabul and Buenos Aires.
subfiles.summary: The data had been prepared by the 2143d Air Weather Wing, U.S. Air Force. The intended recipients were civil or national meteorological authorities in Iran, Mongolia, Afghanistan and Argentina, with a notation that the Mongolian government was not recognized by the United States.

subfiles.title: Letter to the Mongolian Hydro-Meteorological Committee
subfiles.to: President, Hydro-Meteorological Committee, Mongolian People Republic
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese compliance with Resolution XLIII CRII and lists geodynamic reference heights for selected mountain stations.
subfiles.summary: The letter states that compliance began on January 1, 1949. Its table gives index numbers, coordinates, elevations and pressure-reduction heights for ten Japanese stations, including Mount Aso, Mount Fuji, Mount Tateyama and Mount Iwate.

subfiles.title: Transmittal slip for meteorological data to Tehran
subfiles.from: Department of State, Acquisition and Distribution Division
subfiles.about: Forwards Despatch 164 and an envelope of meteorological data for the Chief Meteorologist in Tehran.
subfiles.summary: The embassy was asked to transmit the 2143d Air Weather Wing material if the officer in charge perceived no objection. A copy of the Tokyo despatch accompanied the data.

subfiles.title: Transmittal slip for meteorological data to Buenos Aires
subfiles.from: Department of State, Acquisition and Distribution Division
subfiles.about: Forwards meteorological data to the president of Regional Commission III of Argentina's national weather service.
subfiles.summary: The package consisted of Despatch 164 and an envelope prepared by the 2143d Air Weather Wing. Delivery was conditional on the officer in charge having no objection.

subfiles.title: Transmittal slip for meteorological data to Kabul
subfiles.from: Department of State, Acquisition and Distribution Division
subfiles.about: Forwards duplicate meteorological data for possible delivery to Afghan authorities.
subfiles.summary: The slip transmits a copy of Tokyo Despatch 164 and data prepared by the 2143d Air Weather Wing. The embassy was authorized to deliver the material if it perceived no objection.

subfiles.title: SCA recommendation on transmitting data to Afghanistan
subfiles.to: Philip G. Strong, IAD, attention Miss Willink
subfiles.about: Recommends discretionary delivery of Japanese meteorological data to Afghan authorities through the embassy in Kabul.
subfiles.summary: SCA found no reason to deny the material to interested authorities in Kabul. It advised sending the data to the embassy with instructions that delivery remain at the embassy's discretion and returned Despatch 164 with two data copies.

subfiles.title: IAD request for guidance on Afghan meteorological data
subfiles.to: Elbert G. Mathews, SOA, attention Mr. Leach
subfiles.about: Requests a policy decision on whether data addressed to the Afghan Meteorological Service should be sent through the embassy in Kabul.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum follows a telephone conversation between Mr. Frye and Miss Willink. It attaches Tokyo Despatch 164 and the envelope intended for the Director of the Afghan Meteorological Service.

subfiles.title: Record-copy replacement notice for Tokyo Despatch 164
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Communications and Records
subfiles.about: Designates an attached copy of Despatch 164 as the official record copy because the original action copy was not returned.
subfiles.summary: The form identifies Tokyo Despatch 164 under file 894.9243/3-2149. It orders that the substitute record copy be returned to DC/R for filing.

subfiles.title: Information copy of Tokyo Despatch 164
subfiles.from: Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Duplicates the request to distribute four packages of meteorological information internationally.
subfiles.summary: This copy again names the intended recipients in Tehran, Ulaanbaatar, Kabul and Buenos Aires. It is marked as an information copy for divisional retention rather than return to central records.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about relocating Ocean Weather Station X-Ray
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Asks whether a Japanese ship at Station X-Ray could move eastward and eliminate the need for a U.S. ship at Station J.
subfiles.summary: The Bureau of the Budget proposed moving the Japanese weather ship ten degrees east from its stated position of 42°N, 151°E. The Department asked SCAP to consider whether this could replace the American vessel at Station J, given as 45°N, 165°E.

subfiles.title: Tokyo response on North Pacific weather-station operations
subfiles.about: Argues for continued weather-ship coverage between Japan and the Aleutians and reports consideration of Japanese replacement of U.S. ships.
subfiles.summary: Tokyo supplied operating-position information and judged continued coverage between Japan and the Aleutians highly desirable. SCAP was considering a recommendation that Japanese ships replace U.S. ships assigned to Station J without altering the existing pattern of operations.

subfiles.title: Authorization for Japanese operation of Stations J and X-Ray
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports Navy and Coast Guard approval of Japanese operation of both ocean weather stations and requests a takeover of Station J by October 1.
subfiles.summary: The Department stated that the Navy would cease operating Station J on October 1. SCAP was asked to arrange a Japanese takeover by that date if possible; the message was cleared by Navy Captain E. Grant and Coast Guard Captain H. C. Moore.

subfiles.title: Department telegram on absence of funds for Station J reimbursement
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Explains that the Navy had not planned to reimburse Japan for operating Station J and had stopped negotiations because funds were unavailable.
subfiles.summary: Responding to the August 16 Army message, the Department said the Navy did not contemplate reimbursing Japan. COMNAVFE had been instructed not to negotiate without funding, and SCAP received a copy of those instructions; the date and identification as State telegram 420 are supplied by the September 3 reply.

subfiles.title: Army message authorizing reimbursable Station J negotiations
subfiles.to: Secretary of State and other U.S. authorities
subfiles.about: States that there was no objection to Japanese operation of Station J on a reimbursable basis and authorizes direct contract negotiations.
subfiles.summary: The message cites earlier Navy correspondence and State telegram 378. Despite severe OCR corruption in the routing and command names, its substantive point is that Japanese operation was acceptable if reimbursed and that direct negotiation of a contract was authorized.

subfiles.title: Tokyo argument that Station J is a U.S. commitment
subfiles.to: Department of the Army, with information to Department of State
subfiles.about: Urges continued operation of Station J, asks whether Coast Guard funds are available and estimates the cost of reimbursing Japanese operators.
subfiles.summary: Tokyo emphasized that Station J furnished essential information for air-sea rescue on established air routes and traced the requirement to the 1948 North Pacific regional air-navigation meeting in Seattle. It argued that Navy practice and Public Law 738 made the station a U.S. commitment, while noting that Japanese operation was feasible on a fully reimbursable basis. The estimated annual requirement appears to be $400,000, although the OCR renders the amount as “3400,000.”

interest: The most distinctive item is SCAPIN 1782, an unusually detailed snapshot of the physical and administrative infrastructure of Japanese meteorology immediately after the war: it identifies almost 200 stations, their elevations, service codes, instrumentation and reporting obligations. The file also shows weather data functioning as a form of early postwar international scientific exchange, including with an unrecognized Mongolian government and with Afghanistan. Finally, the Station J correspondence exposes the strategic and financial dimensions of ocean meteorology, linking routine weather observations to trans-Pacific aviation, air-sea rescue, occupation policy and the contested transfer of American responsibilities to Japanese vessels.
